title: Proteomics of Prostate Cancer Tissue Small Extracellular Vesicles Reveal Alteration of Metabolism
projectDescription: Prostate cancer (PCa) is a leading male malignancy worldwide, with metabolic reprogramming being a critical hallmark of its progression. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from tissues directly reflect the tumor microenvironment, offering unique insights into cancer pathophysiology that are unattainable through cell line or biofluid-derived EVs. However, the functional roles of tissue-derived EVs in PCa metabolism remain poorly understood. Leveraging our expertise in murine PCa model establishment and EV isolation from prostate tissue, this study aimed to characterize functional differences between PCa and normal prostate tissue via proteomic analysis of tissue-derived small EVs (sEVs). We orthotopically implanted luciferase-labeled PCa cells into nude mice to establish an in situ PCa model, confirmed tumor formation via in vivo imaging, and harvested tissues after four weeks. sEVs were isolated using ultracentrifugation combined with an iodixanol density cushion and characterized by transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and protein marker profiling. Proteomic analysis identified 28 upregulated and 24 downregulated proteins in PCa-derived sEVs compared to normal controls. Subcellular localization revealed enrichment in the cytoplasm, while pathway analysis highlighted significant involvement in metabolic processes, particularly glycolysis, amino acid biogenesis, carbon metabolism, and pyruvate metabolism. Our study establishes a robust method for isolating prostate tissue sEVs and provides the first evidence that PCa tissue-derived sEVs exhibit profound metabolic pathway alterations. These findings enhance our understanding of PCa progression mechanisms and may facilitate the development of novel diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic strategies targeting metabolic dysregulation in PCa.
sampleProcessingProtocol: The differential expression of proteins was determined using label-free quantitative proteomic analysis conducted by EchoBio (Beijing, China), as previously documented. Briefly, 50 µg of purified prostate tissue small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) were lysed in a buffer containing 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate (NH4HCO3) and 8 M urea at pH 8, followed by ultrasonication on ice. The lysate was then centrifuged, and the supernatant underwent reduction with dithiothreitol (DTT) and subsequent alkylation with iodoacetamide. The samples were then mixed with acetone at a ratio of 1:4 and incubated at -20°C for 2 hours. Following centrifugation, the precipitate was collected and washed with cold acetone. The resulting pellet was dissolved in 0.1 M triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) and 8 M urea. Protein concentration was assessed using the BSA standard curve with the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Scientific, USA). Subsequently, 20 µg of protein sample was separated via 12% SDS-PAGE, and the protein bands were stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue R-250. The protein samples, dissolved in a DB proteolysis solution (8 M urea, 100 mM TEAB, pH 8.5), were digested with trypsin (at a ratio of 50:1 for protein to trypsin) in 100 mM TEAB buffer for 4 hours in 37℃, followed by an additional digestion with trypsin and calcium chloride (CaCl2) overnight. Afterwards, the mixture was acidified by formic acid and centrifuged at 12000 g for 5 minat to terminated digestion. The achieving supernatant was desalinated by a C18 desalting columns.
dataProcessingProtocol: The lyophilized protein powder was reconstituted in 10 μL of 0.1% formic acid in water (designated as solvent A) and subsequently subjected to centrifugation. A 1 μg aliquot of the resulting supernatant was injected into a custom-fabricated pre-column (dimensions: 4.5 cm × 75 μm, particle size: 3 μm). Peptide separation was achieved using a custom-fabricated analytical column (dimensions: 15 cm × 150 μm, particle size: 1.9 μm) with a mobile phase consisting of 0.1% formic acid in 80% acetonitrile (referred to as solvent B). Elution of the sample was conducted at a flow rate of 600 nL/min, with the concentration of solvent B being linearly increased from 6% to 100% over a 60-minute period. The column temperature of the precolumn and analysis column is 50℃. The separated peptides were subsequently analyzed using a Q Exactive Series mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a Nanospray Flex™ ion source (electrospray ionization, ESI). The spray voltage was set to 2.1 kV and the ion transfer tube temperature was set to 320°C. The mass spectrometry was performed in data-dependent acquisition mode, with the full scan range of 350-1500 m/z. The resolution of the first stage mass spectrometry was set to 60,000 (200 m/z). The top 40 ions with the highest intensity in the full scan were selected for fragmentation using higher energy collisional dissociation (HCD). The second-stage resolution was set to 15,000 (200 m/z), with a dynamic exclusion time of 20 seconds. The raw data of mass spectrometry were searched using the software Proteome Discoverer 2.2 (PD2.2, Thermo) against the UniProt database (http://www.uniprot.org). The mass tolerance for precursor ions was set to 10 ppm, and for fragment ions, it was set to 0.02 Da, with up to 2 missed cleavage sites allowed. Proteins were considered identified if they contained at least one unique peptide. The search results were further filtered by Proteome Discoverer 2.2 software: Peptide Spectrum Matches (PSMs) with a credibility of more than 99% were considered as credible PSMs, and FDR verification was performed to remove peptides and proteins with FDR greater than 1%.
